title: Best Laptop and Portable Lightweight Ultrabook in 2026
text:
## The best budget laptops and thin-and-light ultrabooks

While the market offers compact laptops that range from several hundred to several thousand dollars, most of you are looking to maximize the return of your money, and my years of experience show me that the sweet spot for that is somewhere in the $700 to $1000 price range or local equivalents in your area.

Shopping at the higher limit of that budget would allow you to get versatile mid-specced variants of some of the premium ultrabooks mentioned earlier (such as the Apple MacBook Air M2, Asus Zenbook 14, Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 and ThinkPad T14).

There are, however, some excellent-value options to consider at the lower end as well, in the $500 to $1000 price range, and we’ll go over them down below, listed alphabetically.

### Acer Swift Go

The Acer Swift Go is one of the best-selling lineups of thin-and-light laptops for the last many years, and a direct follow-up of the even more popular Swift 3 series. Over the years, Acer refined this series into mature and uncompromised products, while keeping prices competitive.

The Swift Go series is available in a multitude of options, in 14 and 16 inch clamshell formats. They’re built alright and ergonomic, and offer the latest features and specs available today. That means you will find these laptops with either IPS or OLED displays, and AMD, Intel or Snapdragon hardware. They tend to offer better performance than the average thin-and-light, due to the higher power settings and beefier cooling, but at the same time implement 54 to 65 Wh batteries, smaller than the segment’s average.

...

### Apple MacBook Air M1

While this is an older design and doesn’t look as exquisite as the updated Air M2-M4 models, the Air M1 is still a fair option if you can snag it for around 500 USD/EUR or less.

It’s still a sturdily built unibody aluminum laptop with decent performance for daily use and excellent battery life, as well as good inputs. The IO is minimalist and the display is average at best, with an older-gen IPS panel and chunky bezels, but these could be compromises worth having when shopping on a tight budget.

title: HP OmniBook 5 review: The MacBook Neo alternative to beat | Tom's Guide
text:
The HP OmniBook 5 14 impresses thanks to its lovely design, sharp OLED panel, strong performance, and astonishing battery life. Though it lacks HDR and has a so-so webcam, it’s a worthy alternative to the MacBook Neo for Windows users.

...

The HP OmniBook 5 has modest specs fitting its price. The $649 starting configuration has an Intel Core 5 315 “Wildcat Lake” chip, 8GB of RAM, 256GB of SSD storage, and lacks a touchscreen. Our $749 review unit is a step up, packing an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a touch display.

This laptop is designed to handle the basics, such as web browsing, working in word processors, and streaming videos. I had no problem using HP’s notebook for my everyday work, which usually involves a dozen open Chrome tabs, light photo editing in GIMP, and the occasional YouTube video running in the background.

 Performance benchmarks 

| Header Cell - Column 0 | HP OmniBook 5 | Dell XPS 13 (2026) | MacBook Neo |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Geekbench 6 (single/multi-core) | 2583 / 7855 | 2570 / 8136 | 3535 / 8920 |
| Handbrake (mins: secs) | 11:03 | 10:08 | 9:57 |
| Blackmagic SSD test (write/read) | 2111 / 3469 | 3714 / 5026 | 1440 / 1585 |

As you can see above, the HP OmniBook 5 fares well against similarly-priced budget laptops. In the Geekbench 6 CPU benchmark, its single- and multi-core scores are fairly close to the Dell XPS 13, which has the same Wildcat Lake processor and amount of memory. However, its SSD speeds (Blackmagic) and Handbrake (video transcoding) scores are noticeably lower.

Even though the MacBook Neo we reviewed has only 8GB of RAM, it still outperforms both of its Wildcat Lake-powered rivals by a large margin. The only area where Apple’s affordable MacBook lags is SSD speed. That says a lot about the rock-solid performance the Neo delivers.

 Graphics & gaming benchmarks 

| Header Cell - Column 0 | HP OmniBook 5 | Dell XPS 13 (2026) | MacBook Neo |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3D Mark Wildlife Extreme (score/fps) | 2922 / 18 | 2995 / 17.9 | 3661 / 21.9 |
| Borderlands 3 | 10.5 fps | 10.7 fps | 9.6 fps |

Wildcat Lake is perfect for basic tasks, but it’s decidedly not built for graphically demanding gaming. In the 3DMark Wildlife Extreme test, which measures a machine’s graphical performance, the HP OmniBook 5 scored 2922 and averaged 18 frames per second.

That’s similar to the Dell XPS 13, though the MacBook Neo has an edge over both. Using its built-in benchmark tool, Borderlands 3 is unplayable at 10.5 fps at 1080p. The same is true for the Dell XPS 13 and MacBook Neo.

title: HP OmniBook 5 review: A surprisingly premium MacBook Neo rival | PCWorld
text:
At $699.99, the OmniBook 5 has a lot going for it, including an all-metal chassis and superb battery life. It’s not without its compromises, though. The base configuration just comes with 8GB of non-upgradeable RAM and 256GB of storage.

...

## HP OmniBook 5: Performance

The first thing to note is that the HP OmniBook 5 is a perfectly fast laptop for the stuff you do on a day-to-day basis, like checking your inbox or dropping numbers into a spreadsheet. Its Intel Core 5 320 processor doesn’t suffer much at all here. This is reflected in its PCMark 10 score of 5,341 and UL Procyon Office Productivity score of 4,660–both of which assess how well a laptop handles productivity workloads. 

The graphics performance is a bit of a different story, though. The integrated Intel graphics aren’t powerful. It managed a Time Spy score of 1,655. That’s not a great score, but I also don’t hold the OmniBook 5 to the same standard as I would with a gaming laptop. The OmniBook 5 isn’t a powerhouse nor was it designed to be.

The processor also delivered a Cinebench 2026 multi-thread score of 1,548 points and a single-thread score of 382 points. This basically tells me that it’s a good laptop for daily productivity, but probably not something more demanding like photo editing. 

Now let’s get into some comparisons and see how the OmniBook 5 stacks up against similar machines.

...

First, the Dell XPS 13. Aside from having more storage (512GB) than the OmniBook, they’re pretty much identical as far as hardware goes. It pulls ahead in the UL Procyon Office Productivity benchmark with a score of 6,391. This could be due to a better thermal system or faster memory. 

Then there’s the Acer Swift Air 14. Interestingly, it performed significantly better in PCMark 10 with a score of 7,046 compared to the OmniBook 5’s 5,341. That’s roughly a 32 percent difference, giving the Acer a noticeable advantage in this benchmark. This just goes to show you that two laptops with nearly identical hardware can perform differently. Differences in thermal management and memory configuration could play a role here, though it’s difficult to pinpoint the exact reason.

...

The HP OmniBook 5 is a surprisingly premium laptop for $699.99. I love its lightweight metal construction, stunning OLED display, and excellent battery life. It’s totally capable of handling daily activities, too.

My biggest qualm is the hardware configuration. 8GB of non-upgradeable RAM and just 256GB of storage feel a bit limiting for a laptop at this price, even in this price-crazed AI-fueled world. The Dell XPS 13 and the Acer Swift Air 14, for example, are similarly priced and have more storage. 

Still, there’s a lot to like here. If you’re looking for a lightweight everyday laptop with a beautiful display and long battery life, the OmniBook 5 is worth considering. Just be mindful of its memory and storage limitations.
